title: Coupled Copper-Zinc Catalysts for Electrochemical Reduction of Carbon Dioxide
abstract: A catalyst plays a key role in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to valuable chemicals and fuels. Hence, the development of efficient and inexpensive catalysts has attracted great interest in both academic and industrial communities. The Cu to Zn ratio in the catalysts can be easily tuned by adjusting the precursor solutions. Abstract
A catalyst plays a key role in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to valuable chemicals and fuels. Hence, the development of efficient and inexpensive catalysts has attracted great interest in both academic and industrial communities. In this work, low-cost catalysts coupling Cu and Zn are designed and prepared with a green microwave-assisted route. The Cu to Zn ratio in the catalysts can be easily tuned by adjusting the precursor solutions. The obtained Cu-Zn catalysts are mainly composed of polycrystalline Cu particles and monocrystalline ZnO nanoparticles. The electrodes with optimized Cu-Zn catalysts show enhanced CO production rates of approximately 200 μmol h -1 cm -2 with respect to those with a monometallic Cu or ZnO catalyst under the same applied potential. At the bimetallic electrodes, ZnO-derived active sites are selective for CO formation and highly conductive Cu favors electron transport in the catalyst layer as well as charge transfer at the electrode/electrolyte interface.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Nowadays, global warming and CO2 emissions as well as atmospheric CO2 concentration are central topics in politics and scientific debate. While finding alternative energy sources to fossil fuels can be a good strategy to mitigate new CO2 release, transformation of CO2 into valuable chemicals and fuels through appropriate processes can decrease the current enormous amount of atmospheric CO2. Among many approaches, electrochemical conversion presents several advantages. Firstly, this method can use green chemicals as electrolytes and electricity from renewable energy sources, thus not contributing to new CO 2 emissions while transforming it [1] . Secondly, the products and conversion rates can be tuned by utilizing different catalysts and applying various potentials [2, 3] . Finally, the electrolyzer and electrolysis process for CO2 conversion can be developed based on the already existing

technologies such as water electrolyzers, polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cells, solid oxide fuel cells and so on [4, 5] . However, compared to other electrochemical reduction reactions such as hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) [6] and oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) [7] , the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) confronts much more complications. One of the biggest challenges is the selectivity for a specific product. The CO2RR involves several proton-assisted multiple-electron-transfer pathways with similar standard potentials, producing carbon monoxide (CO, -0.11 V vs the reversible hydrogen electrode, RHE), formic acid (HCOOH, 0.0 V vs RHE, pH  7) [8, 9]
, methane (CH4, +0.17 V vs RHE), ethylene (C2H4,
+0.08 V vs RHE), methanol (CH3OH, +0.02 V vs RHE) and many other products [10, 11] . In addition, the HER (0.0 V vs RHE) competes with the CO2RR in the protic electrolytes. Consequently, it is difficult to inhibit the HER and to obtain satisfactory selectivity for a target product from the CO2RR. Besides the selectivity, another important issue is the overpotential, the difference between the standard and applied potentials. Compared to the HER and ORR, the CO2RR requires much higher overpotentials in order to reach sufficient reaction rates. In addition to the ohmic losses and mass transport limitations, high energy barriers for the activation of CO2 molecules and for the formation of some intermediates significantly contribute to the large overpotential [12, 13] . Besides low energy efficiency, elevated overpotentials can cause other problems such as poor durability of the materials. Hence, catalyst design is essential to decrease the overpotential and to drive the CO2RR selectively and efficiently. In addition, the catalyst itself must be stable under working conditions. Ideally, the precursors and the synthesis of catalyst materials also need to have reasonable costs for purpose of mass-scale implementation. In the recent years, great efforts have been dedicated to material studies and innovations for the electrochemical CO2RR. From both experimental and theoretical studies, gold (Au), silver (Ag), zinc (Zn) and gallium (Ga) are selective for CO formation; indium (In), tin (Sn), lead

(Pb), mercury (Hg) and cadmium (Cd) mainly produce HCOO - ; copper (Cu) shows unique ability to produce a big range of chemicals including alcohols and hydrocarbons beyond CO* [14-16] . Due to its unique feature, Cu is the most studied element and the investigations mainly focus on the effect of the oxidation states of Cu, the influence of the size and shape of the particles and the development of various Cu-based materials including alloys, composites, complexes and so on [13, 17-20] . Particularly, Cu-based bimetallic catalysts attract great interest since their features are highly tunable by changing the type and percentage of the secondary element. Early works showed that alloying Cu with other metals can enhance the selectivity for a specific product and can affect the onset potentials for the formation of some products [21] . Our previous works also revealed that Cu-Sn bimetallic electrodes have an excellent selectivity for CO formation with good activity and stability [22, 23] . Changing the Cu/Sn ratio in the electrode can easily tune the selectivity between CO and HCOO - [24] . Recently, Cu-Zn bimetallic materials are gaining attention since both Cu and Zn are low-cost and environmental-friendly. Zn is even more abundant and much cheaper than Cu, while Cu has electrical conductivity three times higher than Zn. Addition of Zn into the Cu electrode is expected to inhibit the H2 formation due to the low activity of Zn toward the HER [25] . The good conductivity of Cu can reduce the resistance of the catalyst materials and thus enhance mass transport especially at high reaction rates. Yeo et al. [26] prepared Cu-based oxides with different amounts of Zn through electrodeposition for the CO2RR. They found that the selectivity for ethanol (C2H5OH) versus C2H4 production can be tuned by varying the amount of Zn in bimetallic catalysts. Chetty et al. [27] reported that electrodeposition of Zn on Cu substrate can inhibit HER and enhance CH4 formation with faradaic efficiency (FE) of 52%. Miyauchi et al. [28] investigated Cu-Zn alloy materials prepared using vacuum sealing method for electrochemical and photoelectrochemical reduction of CO2. The optimized alloy Cu5Zn8 exhibits good FE values for HCOOH formation, 71.1% in electrochemical CO2RR at -1.0 V

vs. Ag/AgCl and 79.1% in photoelectrochemical CO2RR under UV-light, respectively. The same group also applied Cu-Zn alloy nanoparticles as co-catalyst in visible-light-driven CO2 photoreduction system, yielding HCOOH with FE values over 50% and light energy conversion efficiency of 0.028% [29] . Du et al. [30] reported laser-prepared Cu-Zn alloy catalysts that exhibit an enhanced selectivity for C2H4, with a FE value as high as 33.3% at a potential of -1.1 V vs. RHE. Zhang et al. [31] prepared Cu-Zn bimetallic catalysts with various Zn concentrations by electrodeposition and applied them as cathode materials for the CO2RR, in both electrochemical and photoelectrochemical cells. The optimized Cu-Zn catalyst achieved a good FE value of 60% for HCOOH formation. In the present work, we synthesized Cu-Zn materials through a simple one-pot microwaveassisted route, using copper acetate and zinc acetate as Cu and Zn precursors, respectively. Ethylene glycol was used as the reducing agent. In recent years, the interest in green chemistry has risen greatly. The microwave-assisted synthesis is considered a highly sustainable process due to the high product yields efficiency, the reduction of generated waste, the dramatically decreased time and low energy consumption compared to traditional pyrolysis and hydrothermal methods [32] . Furthermore, this process is scalable for mass-scale production simply by enlarging the reactor and the precursor quantities. Under the microwave radiation at 220 °C, Cu 2+ ions were reduced by ethylene glycol, forming Cu particles. Zn 2+ ions are less noble and were not reduced. Ethylene glycol can strongly coordinate Zn 2+ ions to control particle formation and to prevent nanoparticles aggregation [33] . In fact, we obtained nano-sized ZnO particles without significant agglomerations. In the Cu-Zn samples, distinct morphologies for both Cu and ZnO particles are observed. Various electrochemical techniques were applied in order to evaluate the activity and selectivity of Cu-Zn materials toward the CO2RR. It is revealed that the Cu-Zn samples with optimal compositions achieved good selectivity and activity for the CO production.

sections.heading: 2.1 Materials
sections.text: Copper acetate (Cu(CH3COO)2, 99.9%), zinc acetate dihydrate (Zn(CH3COO)2·2H2O, 99.9%), sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 98%), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, 99.7%), ethylene glycol (EG, 99.8%), Nafion ® 117 solution (5 wt.%) and isopropanol were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Unless otherwise specified, all the materials were used as received.

sections.heading: 2.1 Synthesis of the catalysts
sections.text: The Cu-Zn catalysts were fabricated through a microwave-assisted solvothermal route. Samples containing a single metallic element Cu or Zn were synthesized for the purpose of comparison. The six catalysts, namely Cu, CuZnx (where x is the atomic ratio of Zn/(Cu+Zn) in the precursor solution, Cu-Zn) and ZnO, were prepared with various concentrations of different precursors (Table S1). In a typical synthesis, the Cu and Zn salts were dissolved in 35 mL of EG and 5 mL of H2O to form solution 1, and 914 mg of NaOH was dissolved in 17 mL of EG and 3 mL of H2O to form solution 2. Then, solution 2 was added into solution 1 drop by drop. After 10 min of vigorous agitation, the mixture was then transferred into a Teflon vessel (volume 100 mL). The Teflon vessel was put in a microwave oven (Milestone STARTSynth, Milestone Inc., Shelton, Connecticut) and connected to pressure and temperature probes. The mixture was irradiated for 11 min at 900 W (TMax. = 220 °C), and then was cooled to ambient temperature. The precipitate was separated by centrifuge and washed twice with H2O and once with ethanol. The powder sample was finally obtained by vacuum drying at 60 °C overnight.

Samples were weighted and digested in a flask with 10% of aqua regia overnight, filled up at volume with Milli-Q and filtered using a 0.45 µm PTFE filter before reading them with the instrument. Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, ZEISS Auriga) was used to evaluate the morphology of the materials. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterization was performed with a FEI Tecnai F20ST microscope, equipped with a field emission gun operating at 200 kV. High-angle annular dark field (HAADF) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX, EDAX) detectors were used in Scanning TEM (STEM) mode. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out by using a PHI 5000 VersaProbe (Physical Electronics) system. The X-ray source was a monochromatic Al Kα radiation (1486.6 eV). Spectra were analyzed using CasaXPS Version 2.3.18 dedicated software. All core-level peak energies were referenced to C1s peak at 284.5 eV and the background contribution, in high resolution (HR) spectra, was subtracted by means of a Shirley function. The powder sample was directly attached onto a conductive carbon tape to obtain a complete and uniform layer. No signal from the tape has been recorded during analysis, since Si2p signal coming from the tape has not been detected.

sections.heading: 2.4 Electrochemical tests and product analysis on the prepared electrodes
sections.text:
For each electrochemical measurement, an as-prepared electrode was used. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were performed in a three-electrode cell at room temperature with a CHI760D electrochemical workstation. The working electrode was a catalyst-coated carbon paper with a geometric area of 0.2 cm 2 . A Pt wire was used as counter electrode and Ag/AgCl (3 M NaCl) was used as reference electrode. To study the electrocatalytic performance of the electrodes, CV measurements were performed from +0.4 V to -1.2 V vs RHE at a scan rate of 10 mV s -1
in Ar and CO2-saturated
0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solutions. Unless otherwise specified, all the potentials refer to the RHE in this work. EIS measurements were performed at various potentials from -0.6 V to - 1.2 V with an AC signal of 10 mV of amplitude and 10 -1 - 10 5 Hz frequency range in a CO2saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. CO2 electrolysis was carried out by applying chronoamperometric (CA) technique with a CHI760D electrochemical workstation. The CA experiments were conducted in a customized two-compartment cell with a proton exchange membrane (Nafion™ Membrane N117, Sigma-Aldrich) as the separator, as shown in Scheme S1. The volume of each side was 10 mL with 3 mL of headspace. A mini Ag/AgCl (1 mm, leak-free LF-1) was used as the reference and a Pt foil (3.3×3.3 cm 2 ) as the counter electrode. The working electrode was a catalyst (Cu, Cu-Zn or ZnO)-coated carbon paper with a geometric area of about 1×1.35 cm 2 . A 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution was used as the electrolyte. In the pattern of the ZnO sample, all peaks are associated to ZnO (Zinc oxide, JCPDS 01-075-0576), without additional peaks related to impurities. No significant shifts of the peaks are observed on the XRD patterns of the Cu-Zn materials compared to that of the ZnO sample (Fig. 1b) and the one of the Cu sample (Fig. 1c), indicating the absence of a Cu-Zn bond in the bimetallic samples [34] .
Fig. 2 shows the morphologies of the as-prepared samples at a low and a high magnification with images at an even higher magnification in the insets. As shown in Fig. 2a, the particles in the Cu sample have a wide size distribution from nano to submicron scale (e.g. particles A and B). The microsized particles are dominant and have a rough surface (e.g. particles A and C). It is also noticed that some of them are oriented assemblies of nanoparticles (NPs), evident by the particle D at a higher magnification in the inset. Similar agglomeration phenomenon was also observed in our previous work on Cu-based materials prepared with a similar route [3] . In the synthesis, ethylene glycol (EG), used as the bulk solvent, could play

the role of a surfactant favoring the oriented packing of small Cu particles, as previously reported in other work [35] . The agglomeration of small particles, especially nano-sized ones, could be driven by surface energy reduction [35, 36] and the oriented agglomeration could be included by the EG surfactant. The eventually formed assemblies are reflected as Cu submicron particles as observed in Fig 2a. The ZnO sample consists of round nanoparticles (NPs), as shown in Fig. 2f and its inset. The morphologies of the Cu-Zn samples are shown in Fig. 2b-e. At the low magnification, the CuZn0.1 sample shows a reduction of average particle size compared to the Cu one and it is mainly composed of Cu-like submicron particles. The CuZn0.25 sample seems to have a similar average particle size with the CuZn0.1 sample and a further increase of Zn content in the sample leads to no direct observation of submicron particles in Fig. 1d and 1e at the low magnification. At the high magnification, all Cu-Zn samples display two distinct morphologies, ZnO-like NPs and Culike submicron particles, as shown in Fig. 2b-e as well as Fig. S1-S4. The NPs decoration on the Cu-like particles is observed and marked with red circles in Fig. 2b-e and also highlighted at the higher magnification in the inset of Fig. 2c-e. With increasing the Zn percentage, the surfaces of the Cu-like particles rapidly decrease and those of ZnO NPs rapidly increase on the Cu-Zn sample, due to the fact that nanosized ZnO has a high surface area-to-mass ratio and ZnO NPs decorate on the Cu particles. Additionally, the analysis at high magnification shows no significant changes in the sizes of the visible Cu-like particles and ZnO-like NPs with increasing the Zn percentage in the Cu-Zn samples.

TEM characterization was performed on one selected sample (CuZn0.4) in order to better understand the morphological and structural properties of these materials. Bright field (BF) TEM images shown in Fig. 3a and b confirm that two distinct morphologies are present. There are several large particles and many NPs, attributed to Cu and ZnO respectively. The electron diffraction pattern in Fig. 3c confirms the polycrystalline nature of the sample, the reflections from numerous ZnO planes can be identified along with reflection from Cu (111), which is in agreement with the XRD result. It is important to note that majority of the Cu particles are large and thick, so that they are not electronically transparent. Therefore, only limited signal can be detected from them both in TEM and in selected area electron diffraction (SAED) analysis. The BF-TEM image in Fig. 3b shows an area of the sample,

Therefore, some smaller Cu particles are also present and not easily distinguishable from ZnO NPs. In addition, it is possible to note from the STEM image (Fig. 3e) that the large Cu particle is polycrystalline, which is consistent with FESEM observation. The Cu2p doublet region acquired in high resolution (HR) mode is shown in Fig. 4b. The CuZn0.4 sample shows a typical spectrum related to the mixed oxidation states of Cu, including Cu(0), Cu(I) and Cu(II), with a small satellite due to Cu(II) oxidation state [37] . To overcome the difficulty related with a correct deconvolution procedure of the Cu2p doublet, due to both the presence and overlapping of several satellites and shake-up peaks for each oxidation state, we applied an analysis method developed by Biesinger et al. [37] , which can help to evaluate the ratio between Cu(II) and Cu(0) + Cu(I) by fitting Cu2p3/2 peak and its related satellite (see Fig.4b). By applying this method, we obtained the following values: 34% due to Cu(II) and 66% due to Cu(0) + Cu(I). This result is in accordance with the typical shape of the doublet, since a lower amount of Cu(II) with respect to Cu(0) + Cu(I) is reflected in a low intensity satellite peak at about 942 eV. Cu(0) state is already observed with XRD and TEM, while Cu(I) and Cu(II) are absent in the diffraction analyses, probably due to their low amount or their amorphous phase [23, 38] . The oxides in the upmost layer can be formed due to the exposure to atmosphere [38, 39] . Regarding the Zn oxidation state, both the photoelectronic peak Zn2p3/2 and the Auger ZnLMM peak were analyzed (Fig.4c and d). The first peak has been deconvoluted with two Gaussian-Lorentzian curves (1021.0 eV and 1022.5 eV), obtaining two chemical shift related to ZnO (62.3%) and Zn(OH)2 (37.7%) compounds [40] . sections.heading: 3.2 Electrochemical characterizations and product analyses of the prepared electrodes
sections.text:
The as-prepared catalysts are coated onto a carbon paper in order to obtain the electrodes and to enable the electrochemical evaluation of the materials toward the CO2RR. Each electrode is named as the corresponding catalyst. For example, an electrode composed of monometallic Cu catalyst is denoted as Cu electrode. The electrocatalytic performance of the electrodes toward the CO2RR was firstly studied by using CV in Ar- and CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solutions. Ar or CO2 gas was bubbled through the electrolyte for 30 min before CV tests and the same gas flux was maintained during the measurements. The electrodes were stabilized by performing 30 cycles at a scan rate of 100 mV s -1 before recording the cyclic voltammograms (CVs). Fig. 5a shows the CVs on the Cu electrode. No peaks related to the redox reactions of Cu are observed on the curves in the investigated potential range. In the negative potential range, Cu electrode in the CO2 electrolyte has a lower current density than that in the Ar one at the same potential. Moreover, the onset potential for reduction reactions shifts negatively in the CO2-saturated electrolyte. These observations are in agreement with the reported results on Cu materials for the CO2RR [23, 44] . From the CVs at the ZnO electrode (Fig. 5b), it is evident that Zn starts to be oxidized at -0.5 V and continues to be oxidized at more positive potentials in the anodic scan, while the ZnO is reduced or partially reduced at more negative potentials (< -0.5 V) in the cathodic scan. According to the work reported by Roldán Cuenya et al. [43] , ZnO NPs (1.7 and 3.9 nm) are not completely reduced to metallic Zn even under strongly negative potentials during the CO2RR. Hence, even though the observed reduction peak for the Zn 2+ , we are not able to exclude the presence of cationic Zn species under such negative potentials. The redox reactions of Zn are also present on the CVs at the Cu-Zn electrodes, as displayed

in Fig. S6. It is commonly considered that the comparison of the current densities obtained in Ar- and CO2-saturated electrolytes is indicative of the selectivity of a Cu-based electrode [23, 34] . A catalyst that produces a higher current density in CO2 electrolyte than that in N2 one is usually favorable for the CO2RR with respect to the HER at the corresponding applied potential. Interestingly, each Cu-Zn electrode shows a higher current density in CO2 electrolyte compared with that in N2 one at the potentials from -0.8 V to -1.1 V, as displayed in Fig. S6. In addition, each Cu-Zn electrode shows a different variation between the two current densities (jCO2 – jAr) with a trend CuZn0.4 > CuZn0.5 > CuZn0.25 > CuZn0.1, implying that the selectivity of these electrodes for the CO2RR alters and follows the same trend. Comparing the CVs in the Ar electrolyte (Fig. 5c), in the negative potential range (≤ - 0.8 V) where mainly HER occurs, the Cu electrode displays a much larger geometric current density than the ZnO one, indicating that Cu is much more active than Zn toward the HER, in agreement with the literature [45] . With increasing ZnO percentage in the Cu-Zn material, the corresponding electrode shows a decreased current density. Since the same catalyst loading is used for all electrodes, the one containing a Cu-Zn material with a higher ZnO percentage is expected to have more exposed Zn surface and less exposed Cu surface, according the observations from FESEM analysis (Fig. 2). Hence, the decline of geometric activity of the Cu-Zn electrode with raising the ZnO content is attributed to the increase of less active Zn surface and the simultaneous decrease of more active Cu surface. In the CO2-saturated electrolyte, the Cu-Zn electrodes show a broad peak from -0.8 V to -1.1 V (Fig. 5d), further implying that these electrodes could have notable selectivity for the CO2RR in this potential range.

The impedance spectra acquired at different potentials in the CO2-saturated electrolyte are reported in Fig. 6a-f. The total impedance decreases while moving toward more negative potentials, in agreement with the fast increase in current when lowering the potential in the CVs. The CuZn0.4 and CuZn0.5 electrodes can reach high CO production rates of 201 and 193 μmol h -1 cm -2 , respectively, at -1.1 V. The materials presented herein demonstrate an enhanced selectivity and production rate of CO compared to the reported similar materials [26, 28-31, 47] . To further investigate the stability behavior, 4 h of electrolysis has been performed on a CuZn0.4 electrode at -1.0 V. As shown in Fig. 9c, the CuZn0.4 electrode maintains a quasi-steady CO partial current density of 4.3 mA cm –2 . The FECO retains an average value of 70%, while the FE for H2 yield remains about 28%. The stable activity and selectivity of the electrode indicate the durability of the CuZn0.4 material under very negative potentials. The good performance and remarkable stability of the Cu-Zn materials imply their promising potential for the CO2RR to CO in real devices with continuous operation. CO is an important product from the reduction of CO2 since it has high relevance for the chemical industry [48] . It is considered the most important C1-building block and is intensively used in large industrial processes such as Fischer-Tropsch synthesis of hydrocarbons and Monsanto/Cativa acetic acid synthesis. Since CO is a toxic molecule and inconvenient for transportation, the in-/ex-situ exploitation of CO obtained from electrochemical CO2RR is also studied. Ager et al. [49] reported a sequential cascade pathway to convert CO2 to C2+ hydrocarbons and oxygenates in a two-step electrocatalytic process using insolated CO as the intermediate. Ag or Au catalyst selectively converts CO2 to CO and the nearby Cu catalyst further converts CO to C-C coupled products. CO generated from CO2RR can also be ex-situ used by the integration of the CO2RR process with a follow-up CO utilization process. Skrydstrup et al. [50] reported an operationally simple and scalable electrochemical set-up for the CO production on demand in synthetically useful scales with a commercially available molecular catalyst (iron tetraphenylporphyrin) and its sequential adaptation to palladium catalyzed carbonylation reactions for C-C and C-heteroatom bond

Hence, the CO-selective electrocatalysts can be applied in processes to produce CO for temporary storage or to generate CO on demand for further synthesis of high-value fuels and chemicals. Particularly, our powder-like materials have potential to be implemented in the gas diffusion electrode (GDE), which enables a dramatic improvement in the reaction rates and thus enable the production of CO in industrial scales. The development of the GDE is underway in our lab. The good performance of CuZn0.4 and CuZn0.5 electrodes could be attributed to the balance of ZnO and Cu contents. Large amount of ZnO-derived active sites guarantee good selectivity for the CO formation, since the ZnO electrode has satisfactory CO selectivity as widely reported in the literatures [25, 51, 52] . Sufficient Cu content is necessary to enhance electric conductivity and to obtain high electrode activity. While it is essential to understand the CO2RR to CO reaction pathways to enable the optimization of catalyst design, it is rather difficult to conduct reliable mechanism studies of the CO2RR on metal-based catalysts due to several factors. Firstly, the CO2RR is very complex and involves many possible pathways, even for the simple products such as CO and HCOOH [11] . It is believed that the formation of CO or HCOOH depends on the initial binding mode of the first intermediate of CO2 reduction. The *COOH intermediate that binds to the catalyst via the C atom leads to CO formation, while the HCOO* intermediate that binds to the catalyst through (one of) the oxygen atoms leads to formate or formic acid production. Nevertheless, it is not clear that the formation of *COOH is through a concerted proton-electron transfer or a decoupled protonelectron transfer to CO2. It is also not definite that the HCOO* is formed through a decoupled proton-electron transfer to CO2 or a coupled proton-electron transfer to metal site followed by a CO2 insertion into the metal-H* bond. Secondly, the local environment at/near the active sites where the CO2RR occurs is dependent on the applied potential and the catalyst structure. High overpotentials and insufficient mass diffusion can lead to significant differences between the bulk electrolyte and the local electrolyte at/near the active sites [53] . The OH - generated from the reduction reactions increases the local pH and thus alters the absolute potential and the CO2/HCO3 - /CO3 2- equilibrium, dramatically altering the reaction mechanism and thus the selectivity and activity of the catalyst. A recent study found that even the ratelimiting step is dependent on the applied potentials from experiments and multiscale modeling [54]
. Thirdly, the oxidation state of Zn under the CO2RR, that is, the nature of the
active sites, is not clear. By operando X-ray absorption fine-structure spectroscopy

[25] demonstrated that the nanostructured Zn-based catalyst is reduced to metallic Zn and structurally stable at potentials more negative than -0.7 V through in-situ/operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy measurements. Hence, more studies are necessary to understand the real active sites at the Zn-based catalysts. Due to the above-mentioned uncertainty, the mechanism study of CO2RR must be based on in-situ/operando experiments. By these advanced techniques, it is possible to reveal the real active sites, the formed intermediates and the local environment. Based on such information, it is possible to elucidate the reaction mechanism with good reliability. The mechanism study of CO2RR on Zn-based materials is scarcely reported. By in-situ infrared absorption spectroscopy measurements, Peng et al. [52]
suggested that the CO2RR to CO process on
metallic Zn surface includes four elementary reaction steps: (1) one electron transfers to CO2 to form CO2 *− ; (2) one proton transfers to CO2 *− to obtain COOH * intermediate; (3) an electron and a proton transfer to COOH * to form CO * ; (4) CO * desorbs to produce CO. This is consistent with the CO2RR to CO mechanism at Ag surfaces [55, 56] . While this mechanism is acceptable, the real oxidation state of Zn in the bimetallic Cu-Zn catalyst under the CO2RR condition is not studied and its effect on the reaction mechanism should be taken into consideration. In addition, the effect of coupled Cu on the Zn-based active sites should also be considered. Hence, in-situ/operando experiments will be conducted to correlate the structure/performance relationship and to explore the CO2RR mechanism at the Cu-Zn catalysts.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
Coupled Cu-Zn catalysts have been successfully prepared with a simple and green route. The obtained catalysts have various Cu/Zn atomic ratios, as designed in the experiment. All the Cu-Zn samples show two distinct particle types, nano-sized ZnO and submicron Cu particles. The monometallic Cu electrode exhibits low selectivity for the CO2RR with FECO and FEHCOOH values under 9% and 8%, respectively. In contrast, the monometallic ZnO electrode obtains significantly improved FECO as high as 74% and slightly lower FEHCOOH of 5%. In all

the investigated potential range, the Cu electrode shows much higher activity than the ZnO one. Coupling Cu and Zn can enhance CO selectivity compared to the Cu electrode and can improve the electrode activity with respect to the ZnO one. Consequently, the optimized CuZn electrode achieves a higher partial current density for CO production with respect to the monometallic ones at the same applied potential. The improved performance of the Cu-Zn electrodes is attributed to the selective active sites derived from ZnO and to the high conductivity of Cu. The herein proposed Cu-Zn catalysts are low-cost and the fabrication method is environmentally friendly and energetically convenient, enabling their mass-scale production. These powder-like materials can potentially be implemented in optimized configurations of CO2 electrolysis devices to enable industrial scale production of CO. Hence, our CO-selective electrocatalysts can be applied in large-scale processes to produce CO for further synthesis of energy-dense/high-value fuels and chemicals. The present work highlights the importance of rational design of bimetallic or even trimetallic materials for the CO2RR application. Catalysts with desired characteristics can be obtained by combining different types of metals/metal oxides and by easily tuning their chemical compositions. This work can be an indication for developing efficient and affordable electrocatalysts at largescale production for the CO2 conversion.
